current_leader.name: Merchant settlement acceleration decision engine
current_leader.state_transition: processor balance becomes eligible -> standard settlement ETA and paid acceleration tiers are known -> external cash and obligations determine liquidity needed before each ETA -> recommend zero, same-day, or instant settlement and only the minimum amount -> verify acceleration fees avoided
current_leader.why_survived: Paid settlement acceleration remains an explicit recurring financial choice. Razorpay currently publishes incremental prices for instant and same-day settlement and allows custom settlement rules, but fresh competition searches did not identify an exact product combining processor available balance, standard settlement ETA, acceleration fee tiers, live external liquidity and obligations due before each ETA to compute the minimum economically justified accelerated amount. The intervention can remain read-only and outside the payment path.
current_leader.closest_threat: Razorpay already supports custom settlement rules, and broad treasury/cash-flow products forecast liquidity. A first party or treasury platform could combine those primitives. Gate 8 remains uncertain until exact cash-aware minimum-acceleration functionality is ruled out comprehensively.
current_leader.smallest_intervention: Read processor balance and settlement ETA, acceleration fee tiers, bank balance and obligations due before standard settlement. Output the cheapest sufficient choice: no acceleration, same-day, or instant, plus the minimum amount. V1 does not initiate a payout or hold funds.
current_leader.monetization: Small per valuable settlement decision, low monthly micro-fee, or capped share of verified acceleration fees avoided versus a competent treasury baseline.
current_leader.biggest_unresolved_risk: The avoidable paid-acceleration pool is unquantified. If merchants already accelerate only the exact amount genuinely needed before free settlement, the theoretical fee delta has little real-world volume.
current_leader.next_research_test: Quantify actual unnecessary accelerated-settlement volume using merchant cash-flow examples or processor/merchant disclosures, and search specifically for products that combine PSP balances, bank balances, obligations and settlement-speed fees to recommend the minimum acceleration amount. Kill if avoidable volume is small or an exact incumbent is found.

recent_cross_family_findings: Processor-native currency settlement is rejected on Gate 8: Airwallex now explicitly combines like-for-like settlement, multi-currency holding and direct same-currency supplier/card/payout use, with conversion only when needed. This closed-loop first-party workflow captures most of the proposed double-conversion saving without a separate optimizer.

Merchant settlement acceleration is restored as current leader because paid settlement speed is a recurring explicitly priced decision and no exact cash-aware minimum-acceleration optimizer was found this run.

Dealer warranty labor/parts reimbursement uplift is rejected: Armatus Dealer Uplift already offers turnkey contingent-fee submissions, proprietary optimization software, annual timing tracking and statutory-vs-factory analysis at scale.

Commercial utility tariff/demand optimization is rejected as a broad family: TrueMeter, MeterBase, Vitality and other current systems already perform continuous tariff analysis, demand forecasting, bill auditing and in some cases automated load control with verified savings.

New search rule: Gate 8 considers economic neutralization, not only exact feature naming. If a first-party closed-loop default captures most value, a separate recommendation layer does not have enough whitespace.
Settlement-speed optimization must be benchmarked against competent cash management, not against naively accelerating the entire available balance.
known_rejected_or_demoted_summary: Full historical rejection list is preserved in prior anchor blobs and immutable run files. Do not revive prior rejected families without materially new mechanism/evidence.
